newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgarian election keeps its distance from crisis.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgarian election keeps its distance from crisis.

text.p: The campaigns of the two main candidates in Bulgaria's presidential election on Sunday have scarcely mentioned that the country is on the verge of bankruptcy.
Political outsiders more free to speak their minds are winning the admiration of many voters who say they are the only ones talking any sense.

Bulgaria has been slow to implement politically-unpopular reforms and has the lowest level of foreign investment of any country in the region. A quarter of the country's numerous and insolvent banks are in receivership.

"While people in Poland speak of credit cards, Bulgaria still speaks of credit millionaires," Petar Stoyanov, candidate of the anti-communist Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), told a television debate on the economy on Tuesday.

Outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev, who is not seeking re-election, is from the UDF, while parliament is dominated by the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), which grew out of the former Communist party, ousted in 1989.
The president's powers are largely ceremonial but the election, half way through the government's four-year term, is also an indicator of the two parties' relative popularity.

"I'm going to vote for Boichev and Koulekov to teach the UDF a lesson," said engineer Ljubka Spasova, referring to comedians Hristo Boichev and Ivan Koulekov who are running a satirical campaign for the presidency.
"We're terrified we're going to win," Hristo Boichev told reporters on Monday.

The colourful head of the Bulgarian Businessmen's Bloc, George Ganchev, also has a following among voters who like his populist, no-nonsense style. He polled 17 percent in the 1992 presidential election.

"This red-blue argument will not draw new investors as you cannot provide a favourable business climate," he told the sparring BSP and UDF candidates on Tuesday night. The Socialists' party colour is red, the UDF's is blue.

The central bank is rapidly running out of money to prop up the lev and buy fuel and also wheat -- to replace Bulgarian production which was exported because the world price is higher than the local price.
The bank's foreign exchange reserves fell to $506 million at the end of September from $575 million, and $1.47 billion in September 1995.
"We are living from hand to mouth," one economist told a seminar last weekend which discussed Bulgaria's ability to sustain future debt payments.

Economic indicators offer no glimmer of hope and Bulgaria risks becoming the first country to default on its Brady bonds, U.S. Treasury-backed paper which provides emerging economies with a mechanism for restructuring foreign debt burdens.
Annual inflation is forecast to exceed 200 percent this year, growth is expected to be negative. High interest rates introduced to stabilise the banking system have doubled internal debt.

"The government which now rules has made mistakes above all because it did not start reforms immediately, and because it does not explain the reasons for reform and that Bulgaria has no alternative," and Socialist candidate Ivan Marazov, who is also Culture Minister, told the debate.
The International Monetary Fund has twice delayed a much-needed $115 million second tranche of funding, citing government delays in implementing reforms.
Voters who supported the Socialists over the anti-communist UDF in the last parliamentary elections in December 1994 have found the old ways no more effective in resolving the country's crisis.
"There were hard times in Bulgaria before too, but now the crisis is in each home and each family," said one pensioner who said she bitterly regretted voting for the Socialists.
"Life was difficult in the past, but now it has become impossible...I can't even think how we shall survive the coming winter," said historian Ivana Hristozova, a 42-year-old mother of two.
"After 16 years of schooling my salary as a specialist in a state institute is not enough to pay even my central heating bill," said civil engineer Maya Petrashkova, 29.

Many voters say they are too disillusioned with politicians to bother voting at all. The Constitutional Court was asked to rule this week on the debate over what should happen if turnout was below 50 percent and decided a second round should be held.

Private radios are broadcasting a message from former prime minister Reneta Indzhova, who was barred from standing for the presidency on a technicality, saying all politicians are as bad as each other and urging people not to vote.

"No one can sort out that mess," said student Ivan Christov, 23. "I am not going to vote, I don't even want to stay in this country any more. As soon as I graduate, I will leave for Germany or the Netherlands."
